offer.say: Don't look at me like that, champ. I'm using a hardware store stone. It's fine. It's not fine. My grandfather's stone's in your plant room. Gus borrowed it in 1979 for the ice scraper. Forty-seven years. I never asked for it back. That's how you win with Gus. You don't ask.

options.text: Why didn't you just ask him?
Forty-seven years is a long time to make a point.
The plant room's a mess. Maybe later.

why.say: Because then he'd have won. We had a thing. I won't explain it. It involved a sit spin and a ribbon in 1976. Find the stone.

cheek.say: It's the only way to make a point in this town. Fast points don't stick.

decline.say: Later's fine. The stone's patient. So am I. That's a lie, I'm not patient. But the stone is.

accepted.say: Grey. Leather sleeve. A K on it. If it's got a chip on one end, that's from my grandfather throwing it at a Kessler man in 1931.

p_find.say: Gus hid things where he'd see them every day. He liked looking at things he'd won.

complete.say: That's it. Chip on the end. Kessler man. Huh. He kept it on a nail where he'd see it every morning. Of course he did. Here. Five sharpenings, on the house. Don't tell anyone, they'll all want one.

options.text: What was the thing about the sit spin?
Hang it by Old Bertha, where people can see it.

c_spin.say: 1976. Mill pond. Gus bet me a dollar I couldn't hold a sit spin for ten seconds. I held it for eleven. He paid me with a promise. The stone was his way of keeping it. That's all you're getting, champ.

c_hang.say: By Bertha. Fine. The two oldest things in the shop, side by side. Three, if you count me. Don't count me.

c_thanks.say: Don't thank me. Thank my grandfather's aim.

done.say: Stone's home. Edges are better. You can tell, can't you.
